extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art criticism; art historians; critics; practicing painters interested in aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative principles and standards for appreciating and judging painting (and related arts), focusing on pictorial qualities, duties to medium, and the degree to which a work fuses form and matter. Includes examples drawn from Venetian painters, Leonardo, Giorgione, and broader aesthetic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility to an art's special sensuous material
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art's sensuous material brings a special phase or quality of beauty untranslatable into other arts; a work must fulfil its responsibilities to that special material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic criticism should define the limitations of an art and estimate the degree to which a given work fulfils its responsibilities to its special material. Examples: painting's pictorial charm is distinct from poetical thought or mere technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of true pictorial charm (distinct from poetry or technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: True pictorial charm is neither merely poetical thought nor merely communicable technical skill in colour or design; it is an element unique to painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must note the pictorial charm that lies between poetic idea and technical competence — the inventive handling of pure line and colour that is the pledge of the pictorial gift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive handling of drawing/design
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing (design) — the arabesque of line and the projection of forms from a pictorial temperament — is an essential pictorial quality independent of anatomical exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for distinctive 'arabesque' lines (e.g., Tintoret's flying figures, Titian's forest branches) that make ideas visible as scenes or images; this design can render abstract or poetic ideas pictorially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential pictorial colouring
rubrics_metrics.description: Colouring is an essential pictorial quality — a weaving of light and hue through dress, flesh, and atmosphere that gives a new, tangible physical quality to the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the 'magic conditions of light and hue' (e.g., Titian's Lace-girl) and how colour-staining of the whole fabric elevates the work beyond mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of sensuous delight
rubrics_metrics.description: A great picture must first delight the sense directly; sensuous pleasure is the primary condition which then mediates any higher poetic or intellectual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first test is whether the work delights sensuously like a 'fragment of Venetian glass'; only through this delight can poetry or thought operate effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of subject to pictorial design
rubrics_metrics.description: The given subject (sacred, historical, or narrative) should often serve as a pretext for pictorial work; the compositional and pictorial purpose can legitimately override conventional associations of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Leonardo treating sacred subjects as starting points for trains of sentiment, or Giorgione using moments of everyday life as morsels of pictorial expression; evaluate whether subject is bent dexterously to artistic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of identification of form and matter (musical ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art ideally strives to obliterate the distinction between matter and form so that form becomes the matter and vice versa — an identification analogous to musical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate how completely a work makes the form an end in itself and penetrates every part of the matter; measure its proximity to the musical ideal of perfect identification of form and matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to 'musical law' (art's aspiration toward music)
rubrics_metrics.description: All arts aspire towards the condition of music, where the end is not distinct from the means; evaluate the degree to which a painting approximates this consummate condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work presents one saturated effect where subject and handling are inseparable; rate how far the piece tends toward music's unity of form and matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of material limitations (medium-specific fidelity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists and schools that apprehend the necessary limitations of their medium (e.g., Venetian painters) produce work faithful to the pictorial function and decorative/visual priorities of painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the work respects the peculiar laws of its medium (e.g., painting as decorative space) rather than forcing it into the terms of another art (literary or sculptural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial temperament versus mere technical skill or literary interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish an artist's intrinsic pictorial temperament (inventive line and colour) from mere technical dexterity or a work that is primarily literary/poetical in interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether ideas 'float up as a visible scene' due to temperament, or whether the work relies chiefly on intelligible subject-matter or mechanical technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subject as symbolical language rather than literal depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects may be used not for literal pictorial realisation but as starting points for trains of sentiment or symbolic invention that extend beyond conventional associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the ostensible subject functions as motif or pretext (e.g., Leonardo's Saint John or Saint Anne) and whether this furthers the pictorial effect or obscures it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and scale of subject appropriate to pictorial ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose subjects (e.g., genre scenes, small portable pictures) that serve pictorial design and decorative purpose rather than strictly devotional or didactic aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giorgione's invention of genre (morsels of actual life, refined or idealised) is given as a model: subjects should be congruous with the intended pictorial experience and use (cabinet pictures, decorative panels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony between topography/material detail and informing light or expression
rubrics_metrics.description: In landscape and setting, the informing effect of light or an indwelling expression can unite otherwise commonplace material into a dominant artistic tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether topography is modulated by light and mood (e.g., French riverside vs Swiss valley, Venetian landscape retaining abstract elements) so that material details serve the overall pictorial music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for durability and technique suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical choices (media and methods) must suit the support and desired permanence; inappropriate technique may produce ephemeral effect at the cost of durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Leonardo's use of oil on plaster for the Last Supper allowed refinements but rendered the work less durable; weigh inventive technique against long-term survival and intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical assessment of attribution and historical authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of authorship and reputation should be scrutinised by critical science; attribution affects evaluation and historical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that later criticism has reduced Giorgione's corpus and urged caution: factor provenance, critical methods, and the possibility of imitation or loss when judging a master's oeuvre.
